::: {.callout-note}
## Learning outcomes

**After having completed this chapter you will be able to:**

- Explain what an LLM pack is, and how it differs from the course chapters themselves
- Decide when to use an AI coding assistant during this course, and when not to
- Locate the LLM packs available for this course and the workflow stage each one covers
- Set up an AI coding assistant with the packs, on the course server or on your own computer
- Use a pack to get AI-assisted help on a dataset, while critically checking its output
- Properly attribute a pack's guidance when you use it in your own analysis
:::

::: {.callout-important}
## Exercises without, project work with

Do the exercises in the course chapters **yourself, without an AI assistant**.
They are where you build the judgement this chapter relies on: an assistant's
output is only as useful as your ability to tell whether it is right.

The **project work** is where you can bring in an assistant, and the LLM packs
described below — and, after the course, your own data.
:::

## What is an LLM pack?

So far, every chapter in this course has taught *you* how to analyse single-cell
data. An **LLM pack** targets a different reader: an AI coding assistant —
a tool that can read and write code in your project based on natural-language
instructions — writing analysis code for you, on your project data during the
course, and on your own data after it.

A pack is not a copy of the course material. It keeps the decisions, the
guard rails and the failure modes of a workflow — the things you'd want an
experienced colleague looking over your shoulder to catch — in a form an AI
assistant can act on and be checked against, rather than in a form meant to
teach a human step by step.

This course's packs live in the
[`llm-packs/`](https://github.com/sib-swiss/single-cell-r-training/tree/main/llm-packs)
directory of the course repository. Each pack bundles:

- **`pack.yml`** — what the pack covers, what it doesn't, and when it was last
  checked against current package versions
- **`SKILL.md`** — what the assistant should establish before writing any code
- **`rules/`** — the hard rules, written so they can be checked automatically
- **`reference/pitfalls.md`** and **`reference/citations.md`** — worked
  failures, and a table mapping every substantive claim to its source
- **`implementation/`** — a tested reference implementation to adapt rather
  than reimplement from scratch
- **`validate/`** — a linter you can run yourself on any code an assistant
  writes for you

::: {.callout-warning}
## These are pilots

Every pack above is marked `pilot, unreleased` in its own `pack.yml`. That is
not a formality: it means the pack has not yet been used and evaluated widely
enough to be trusted the way you'd trust a published tool. Use them, but keep
your own critical judgement switched on — the same judgement this course is
trying to teach you in the first place. If something looks wrong, it might be.
:::

## Setting up an AI coding assistant

Many AI coding assistants support some notion of a reusable "skill", "tool"
or "context pack": a folder of instructions and supporting files that the
assistant consults automatically once it's relevant, rather than something
you have to re-explain every time. This course's packs are written to work
with that kind of mechanism. The exact name and folder convention differs
between assistants, but the pack itself is just plain Markdown, YAML and R —
nothing assistant-specific — so any assistant that can read project files
and run R code can use one.

Choose the tab that matches how you follow the course:

::: {.panel-tabset}

### Enrolled in the course

The course server comes with an AI coding assistant already set up for you:
[goose](https://github.com/aaif-goose/goose), connected to a language model
(DeepSeek V4.1 Flash) through the course. You don't need an account or an API
key, and all R packages for the course are already installed.

- Your access has a fixed budget for the whole course. If goose reports that
  the budget is exceeded, ask a trainer.
- It only works on the course server, and stops when the server is shut down
  after the course.
- What you type, and the files goose reads, are sent to the model provider.
  Use it for the course and project data, not for your own unpublished or
  sensitive data.

#### 1. Start goose in your project directory

Open the **Terminal** tab next to the Console (if there is none: **Tools** →
**Terminal** → **New Terminal**), go to the directory you work in for your
project, and start goose:

```bash
cd ~/my_project   # replace with your project directory
goose
```

Type your request at the prompt; type `exit` to leave goose. Before goose
runs a command or changes a file that could do damage, it asks for your
approval — read what it wants to do before you approve it.

#### 2. Ask goose to fetch the packs

goose looks for skills in the `.agents/skills/` directory of the project you
start it in. Paste in this prompt:

```
Set up all of the LLM packs from the SIB single-cell transcriptomics course
(https://github.com/sib-swiss/single-cell-r-training) in this project,
without downloading the whole course repository:

1. In a temporary directory, sparse-clone only the llm-packs folder (not
   llm-packs/_dev, which is authoring material, not a pack), using
   `git clone --filter=blob:none --sparse` followed by
   `git sparse-checkout set llm-packs` and then excluding llm-packs/_dev.
2. In .agents/skills/ in this project (create it if it doesn't exist yet):
   - Copy each pack subfolder (every directory directly under llm-packs/
     except _dev) in as its own subfolder there, not merged together.
   - Also copy llm-packs/ENVIRONMENT.md as a plain file directly into
     .agents/skills/ (a sibling of the pack subfolders, not nested inside any
     one of them) - each pack's SKILL.md links to it with a relative path
     (../ENVIRONMENT.md) that only resolves correctly if it lands there.
3. Remove the temporary clone.
4. Confirm the packs and ENVIRONMENT.md are in place by listing .agents/skills/.
```

::: {.callout-tip collapse="true" title="Making goose's output easier to read"}

goose answers in Markdown, which can be hard to read in the narrow Terminal
pane — especially tables.

- Make the Terminal pane larger, or zoom out in your browser.
- goose uses a light colour theme, to match RStudio's default. If you use a
  dark RStudio theme, type `/t` in goose to switch to its dark theme; goose
  remembers your choice.
- Ask goose to write tables to a CSV file instead of showing them, and open
  the file in R with `View(read.csv("results.csv"))`.
:::

### On your own computer

#### 1. Install an AI coding assistant

Follow the official installation instructions for whichever AI coding
assistant you choose to use — goose, which the course server uses, is one
free and open-source option. You will also need access to a language model
for it, usually an API key or subscription from a model provider, and you pay
for what you use. What you type, and the files the assistant reads, are sent
to that provider, so check its terms before you use it on unpublished or
sensitive data. You do not need anything beyond what the course already uses
on top of that — your own R/Seurat setup (see [Setup](day1-1_setup.qmd)) and
your own data.

Check that assistant's own documentation for how it discovers reusable
skills/tools/context packs, and where it expects to find them in a project —
look for terms like "skills", "custom tools", "project rules" or "context
packs". You'll need that answer for the next step.

#### 2. Install the packages yourself, before involving your assistant

Do this yourself, in your own R console, rather than asking your assistant to
do it — the same command from [Setup](day1-1_setup.qmd):

```r
install.packages("renv")
renv::restore(lockfile = "https://raw.githubusercontent.com/sib-swiss/single-cell-r-training/refs/heads/master/renv.lock")
```

This is the single biggest lever you have over how much of your conversation
with the assistant gets spent on installation rather than your actual
analysis. Every pack's `ENVIRONMENT.md` tells the assistant what to do if it
still hits a missing package, but an assistant that never hits one in the
first place never produces — and you never have to read — a single line of
compiler or download output. Do this before step 3, especially if this is a
brand-new project with none of this installed yet.

#### 3. Ask your assistant to fetch the packs

The packs live in this course's GitHub repository, but you don't need to
clone the whole course material yourself, or even know any `git` commands.
A real analysis usually moves through most of the pipeline — QC, then
normalization, then dimensionality reduction, and so on — so the packs are
designed to be fetched **all at once**: each one stays independently
triggered by its own description, so having all of them in place just means
your assistant automatically reaches for whichever one matches the step
you're on, with nothing extra to re-fetch as you move to the next step.

In the project directory where **your own data** lives, start your
assistant and paste in this prompt:

```
Set up all of the LLM packs from the SIB single-cell transcriptomics course
(https://github.com/sib-swiss/single-cell-r-training) in this project,
without downloading the whole course repository:

1. In a temporary directory, sparse-clone only the llm-packs folder (not
   llm-packs/_dev, which is authoring material, not a pack), using
   `git clone --filter=blob:none --sparse` followed by
   `git sparse-checkout set llm-packs` and then excluding llm-packs/_dev.
2. In the location where you look for reusable skills/tools/context packs
   in this project (create that location if it doesn't exist yet):
   - Copy each pack subfolder (every directory directly under llm-packs/
     except _dev) in as its own subfolder there, not merged together.
   - Also copy llm-packs/ENVIRONMENT.md as a plain file directly into that
     SAME location (a sibling of the pack subfolders, not nested inside any
     one of them) - each pack's SKILL.md links to it with a relative path
     (../ENVIRONMENT.md) that only resolves correctly if it lands there.
3. Remove the temporary clone.
4. Confirm the packs and ENVIRONMENT.md are in place by listing that location.
```

Your assistant will likely ask you to approve the commands it runs (clone,
copy, delete) along the way — that's expected, and worth reading before you
approve them. The end result is the same as copying every pack folder by
hand, but you never had to type a `git` command yourself.

::: {.callout-note title="Only need one stage?"}

If you genuinely only ever need a single pack (say, you're only doing QC on
someone else's already-processed data), you can ask for just that one
instead — substitute step 1's `git sparse-checkout set llm-packs` with
`git sparse-checkout set llm-packs/<pack-name> llm-packs/ENVIRONMENT.md`,
and copy both that one pack folder and `ENVIRONMENT.md` (as a sibling of
it, same placement rule as above) in step 2. This fetches less, at the cost
of having to repeat the whole fetch-and-copy process again the next time
you need a different stage.
:::

:::

## Working with your assistant

### Describe your task in plain language

Start your assistant in that project directory and describe what you want to
do, the same way you would ask a colleague:

> *"I have 10x Genomics data from 3 samples in `course_data/count_matrices`.
> Can you help me load it into Seurat and do QC and cell filtering?"*

If the pack's `SKILL.md` description matches your request, the assistant will
consult it automatically. A well-written pack will then ask you things like
*which species* and *how many samples* before writing any code — exactly the
facts this course has taught you are important to establish first.

### Check the output critically

This is the step a pack cannot do for you. Before you trust any code an
assistant writes:

- Read `reference/pitfalls.md` yourself. It describes, in the pack's own
  words, exactly what can go wrong.
- Run the relevant pack's linter on the code you were given — and remember
  rule 1: that code has to exist as a file first (adjust the path to
  wherever the packs ended up; on the course server that is `.agents/skills/`):

  ```{bash day1-4-llm-packs-1}
  #| eval: false
  Rscript path/to/scrnaseq-qc-filtering/validate/lint_code.R my_analysis.R
  ```

- Check `pack.yml:validity.last_validated` — if it's old or empty, the pack
  hasn't been re-checked against current package versions recently, and the
  assistant should tell you this before giving advice.

### Keep the attribution

A pack that follows this course's conventions will stamp the course's
provenance onto the object it produces, and offer you a ready-to-paste methods
sentence. Keep both — they are there so that using AI assistance doesn't mean
losing track of where your methodology actually came from.

## Using an assistant in your project

A good first task for your assistant is the QC and filtering of your project
data, **from the raw count matrices**, without telling it which thresholds to
use — it should reach for `scrnaseq-qc-filtering` on its own. You did the same
step by hand in [Analysis tools and QC](day1-3_analysis_tools_qc.qmd), so
compare what it asks you, and what it produces, with what you would have done.

Whatever you let the assistant do, you should be able to explain each step of
your analysis, and why it is right for your data, in your project
presentation. Mention where you used the assistant, and what you checked.

::: {.callout-tip collapse="true"}
## What to look out for

A pack that is working as intended should, among other things:

- Ask you to confirm the species before writing any `PercentageFeatureSet`
  call, rather than assuming human
- Refuse to present the thresholds it uses as "standard" or "default", and
  instead show you the distributions first
- Produce code you can run yourself, not just a description of what to do

If it does none of these, that's useful information too — it's a sign the
pack (or the assistant's use of it) still needs work, which is exactly why
these are pilots.
:::

## Limitations and feedback

LLM packs encode *this course's* decisions for *this course's* workflows —
they are not a general substitute for understanding single-cell analysis, and
they will not catch every mistake. If you find a pack giving advice you think
is wrong, outdated, or missing an important caveat, please open an issue on
the [course repository](https://github.com/sib-swiss/single-cell-r-training/issues).
That feedback is exactly what turns a pilot pack into a trustworthy one.
